catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic in Masakin Tuwal. Phonetically, however, stress is attributed to the following types of syllables in decreasing order: 1) syllables with phonetically lengthened vowels, e.g. [ˈŋaːkːo] "to lift, carry" 2) open, word final syllables conatining [a], [e], [i], [o], [u], e.g. [rəˈgo] "to eat" 3) non-final syllables containing [ə], e.g. [ˈŋəgə] "leg" 4) open, word final syllables containing [ə], e.g. [ˈdəndə] "neck". [ms p. 6:] With the exception of /ə/, all vowels have lengthened allophones. (The syllables in which /ə/ occurs also have less stress than the others.) ... /i/ [ɨ] is a somewhat lowered and centralised, close front vowel. It occurs rhythm group finally and preceding semivowel ... [iː] is a lengthened close front vowel, occuring non-finally in the rhythm group, except before semi-vowel
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and assigned by syllable type: prominence goes preferentially to a syllable whose full vowel is (positionally) lengthened -- full vowels /i e a o u/ are long when non-final in the rhythm group and short finally -- otherwise to an open word-final syllable with a full vowel, then to a non-final schwa syllable, and last to a final schwa syllable; schwa is never lengthened and its syllables are the least stressed. In effect prominence tracks vowel length/quality rather than a fixed edge (initial in [ˈŋaːkːo], [ˈŋəgə], [ˈdəndə]; final in [rəˈgo]).
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the author does not say which syllable wins when a word has several lengthened full vowels, and notes the tone analysis is inconclusive (a few tonal minimal pairs, e.g. [dí] 'fire' vs [dì] 'thorn').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonetic stress, illustrated on citation forms. Vowel lengthening (the top-ranked stress attractor) is defined relative to the 'rhythm group' (2-6 syllables, often several words): word-final full vowels are short group-finally but lengthen group-medially (ms p. 23), so prominence in connected speech may differ from isolation forms. Language also has (poorly analysed) lexical tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Masakin Tuwal (self-name Arra, language Darra), Glottolog dialect masa1303 of Ngile [jle] ngil1242, from Tuwal speakers living in Khartoum (main informant Isa Mehenna, 1981-83), 'with an occasional comparison to Masakin Gusar' (masa1302). Norton & Alaki 2015 treat Tuwal and Daloka-Aheimar (= Ngile proper, Schadeberg's 'Ngile' = Daloka village, dalo1239/ahei1238) as two varieties sharing ISO jle (80% lexical similarity) whose separate-language status is undecided; no stress statement exists for the Daloka/Aheimar dialects themselves.

new_statements.quote: 2a. Tone. The importance of Tone has not yet been fully investigated. A few lexical Tone doublets have been recorded, e.g.: LARO (K-M) yore axes; yore fences MASAKIN ti thorn; ti fire; di egg; di thigh. 2b. Stress. According to Stevenson 'dynamic Stress, accompanied by High or Low tone, plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in all languages'. Examples are not marked for tone or stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Crocker 1984 statement (stress non-phonemic, phonetic prominence by vowel length); adds that stress in the group is 'dynamic' and accompanied by tone, and that Masakin has a few lexical tone doublets (Crocker likewise found a few tonal pairs, analysis inconclusive). Gives no placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the weight-sensitive reading. It is group-level and second-hand (Stevenson 1956-57), and the lect behind T&B's 'MASAKIN' (Stevenson's material, WALS msk) is not identified in the snippets. Opened as full-text-search snippets only: the archive.org item is lending-only (access-restricted, not reachable by automated download); HathiTrust search…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement covering Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa, quoted second-hand from Stevenson: a dynamic (intensity) stress co-occurring with High or Low tone is more important than syllabic pitch as such, but not equally prominent in every language of the group; a few lexical tone doublets are cited for Masakin (ti 'thorn' / ti 'fire', di 'egg' / di 'thigh'). No statement of where word stress falls; examples are not marked for tone or stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the authors note only that stress is 'not equally prominent in all languages' of the group
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's 'MASAKIN' is Stevenson's Masakin material (WALS msk), lect not specified in the snippets; the existing Crocker 1984 statement is explicitly Masakin Tuwal (Darra) = masa1303, a dialect of Ngile ngil1242.
